## Source

Anthropic engineering blog post, *"Effective Harnesses for Long-Running Agents,"* published Nov 26, 2025 (written by Justin Young). The post describes Anthropic's internal experiments running Claude (specifically frontier coding model **Opus 4.5**) on the **Claude Agent SDK** in a loop across many context windows, and the failure patterns observed before they added their two-part harness solution.

## The task

Claude was set up to work autonomously as a long-running agent, operating in **discrete sessions across multiple context windows**, each new session starting "with no memory of what came before." The post likens this to "a software project staffed by engineers working in shifts, where each new engineer arrives with no memory of what happened on the previous shift."

The concrete task: given only a **high-level prompt** — e.g., *"build a clone of claude.ai"* — autonomously build a **production-quality, full-stack web app**. The SDK already provided context-management features such as **compaction**, which in theory should let an agent work "for an arbitrarily long time."

## What the agent did and where it broke down

The post reports that, out of the box (before the harness fixes), "even a frontier coding model like Opus 4.5 running on the Claude Agent SDK in a loop across multiple context windows will fall short of building a production-quality web app if it's only given a high-level prompt." The failures manifested in several observable patterns:

**1. One-shotting the app (early sessions).** "The agent tended to try to do too much at once — essentially to attempt to one-shot the app." Rather than working feature-by-feature, it attempted to build everything in one go.
- **Signal/consequence:** "Often, this led to the model running out of context in the middle of its implementation, leaving the next session to start with a feature half-implemented and undocumented." The post notes "this happens even with compaction, which doesn't always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent."

**2. Lost state on session handoff (subsequent sessions).** Because work was left half-done and undocumented, "the agent would then have to guess at what had happened, and spend substantial time trying to get the basic app working again."

**3. Premature declaration of completion (later sessions).** "A second failure mode would often occur later in a project. After some features had already been built, a later agent instance would look around, see that progress had been made, and declare the job done" — i.e., it stopped while the app was still incomplete.

**4. Marking features done without real testing.** "Claude's tendency to mark a feature as complete without proper testing." The observable behavior: "Absent explicit prompting, Claude tended to make code changes, and even do testing with unit tests or `curl` commands against a development server, but would fail [to] recognize that the feature didn't work end-to-end." So the agent did take real verification-like actions (unit tests, `curl` against a dev server) but those actions did not catch that the feature was broken from a user's perspective.

## Signals/feedback and the harness changes

The post then describes the fixes (initializer agent producing `init.sh`, a `claude-progress.txt` log, an initial git commit, and a JSON `feature_list.json`/`tests.json` with ~200 features marked `"passes": false`; a coding agent working one feature at a time, committing to git, and updating progress). The relevant observable point for the failure: once Claude was **explicitly prompted to use browser-automation tools (Puppeteer MCP) and test "as a human user would,"** it "mostly did well at verifying features end-to-end," and screenshots taken through Puppeteer let it "identify and fix bugs that weren't obvious from the code alone."

## Residual failure even after the fix

One bug class persisted: "Claude can't see browser-native alert modals through the Puppeteer MCP, and features relying on these modals tended to be buggier as a result" — a limitation tied to Claude's vision plus the browser-automation tooling, leaving modal-dependent features buggy.

## Final outcome

The post frames these as the motivating failures that the new harness was designed to solve. With the two-part harness (initializer + incremental coding agent, feature list, progress file, git commits, browser-based end-to-end testing), Claude could make incremental progress across many context windows, and a typical session would begin by running `pwd`, reading `claude-progress.txt` and `feature_list.json`, checking `git log`, restarting the dev server via `init.sh`, and running a basic end-to-end smoke test before starting new work. Some limitations (e.g., invisible alert modals) remained unresolved, and the post lists open questions (single general-purpose agent vs. specialized multi-agent architectures; generalizing beyond web-app development).

Note: the source describes **recurring failure patterns observed across many experimental runs**, not a single annotated trajectory, so individual tool-call logs for one specific failing run are not provided beyond the illustrative session-startup transcript.

We looked to human engineers for inspiration in creating a more effective harness for long-running agents. As AI agents become more capable, developers are increasingly asking them to take on complex tasks requiring work that spans hours, or even days. However, getting agents to make consistent progress across multiple context windows remains an open problem. The core challenge of long-running agents is that they must work in discrete sessions, and each new session begins with no memory of what came before. Imagine a software project staffed by engineers working in shifts, where each new engineer arrives with no memory of what happened on the previous shift. Because context windows are limited, and because most complex projects cannot be completed within a single window, agents need a way to bridge the gap between coding sessions. We developed a two-fold solution to enable the Claude Agent SDK to work effectively across many context windows: an initializer agent that sets up the environment on the first run, and a coding agent that is tasked with making incremental progress in every session, while leaving clear artifacts for the next session. You can find code examples in the accompanying quickstart. The long-running agent problem The Claude Agent SDK is a powerful, general-purpose agent harness adept at coding, as well as other tasks that require the model to use tools to gather context, plan, and execute. It has context management capabilities such as compaction, which enables an agent to work on a task without exhausting the context window.
